notes.title: Start here: syncing lesson progress without losing any
notes.body:
Mobiletagalog is a React Native (Expo) app for learning Tagalog. Progress is stored as a *baseline* from the server plus a local *outbox*: a queue of events (lesson finished, and so on) saved in SQLite on the phone, waiting to be sent. A sync sends part of the outbox and gets a new baseline back. The hard part: the learner keeps using the app, and may even log out, while a sync is still in flight.

Reading order, from the course README:

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: the four files that matter.
2. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: generations versus user identity.
3. `astraupskill/03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: one sync attempt from start to finish.
4. `astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: the 10 tests and the mutations they miss.
5. `astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md`, then `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` (which also lists five review findings).

The core file is `src/lib/sync.ts`, about 100 lines. Read `ProgressSyncCoordinator` slowly, especially `sync()` and `runOnce()`.

excerpts.quote: Progress is a server baseline plus a local outbox of events in device SQLite.
They do not run an Expo device or prove native SQLite durability.

readMore.why: The full reading order with a one-line summary of each chapter.
The four files with line ranges, and two facts about the production push adapter.

notes.title: What a session 'generation' is
notes.body:
The coordinator keeps a number called `generation`. Every call to `setSession` (log in, log out, switch account) adds 1 to it. When `sync()` is called, it remembers the generation at that moment (`requestedGeneration`).

Later, at several points, `runOnce` compares the remembered number with the current one. If they differ, the session that asked for this sync has ended, so the work is abandoned. Think of it as a ticket number: a reply carrying an old ticket number is ignored, even if the same person is standing at the counter again.

While you read `runOnce`, mark every line that compares `requestedGeneration` with `this.generation`, and write next to each one what would go wrong if it were removed. The concepts guide says which of those checks the existing tests actually exercise.

excerpts.quote: setSession(tokens: AuthTokens | null): void { this.generation += 1; this.tokens = tokens; }
const requestedGeneration = this.generation;

readMore.why: Draw the A/B/logout timelines by hand.

notes.title: The outbox, acknowledgements and one SQLite transaction
notes.body:
A sync takes a batch of events from the outbox and sends it. The server answers with new progress and a list of *acknowledged* ids: events it has dealt with. Only then may those events be deleted from the outbox.

Two things must stay in step on the phone: the new baseline, and the removal of acknowledged events. If the app crashed between saving one and doing the other, progress could be counted twice or lost. `commitSyncedProgress` in `src/lib/storage.ts` does both inside `db.withTransactionSync`, so SQLite applies them together or not at all.

Meanwhile the learner can finish another lesson, adding a new event while the request is in flight. Before the quizzes, trace in `runOnce` (lines 83-103) how big a batch is, which ids are allowed to be deleted, and what list is shown to the screen after the commit.

excerpts.quote: /** Atomically adopt server progress and acknowledge only included events. */ export function commitSyncedProgress(baseline: unknown, acknowledgedIds: string[]): void { db.withTransactionSync(() => {

notes.title: Why the tests never notice a missing generation check
notes.body:
**Key: because no test re-logs in as the same user, which the user-id half misses.**

Line 99 has two halves joined by `||`: the generation changed, *or* the current user id differs from the one the sync started with. The existing tests only switch to a different user or log out. In both cases the user id no longer matches, so the second half already stops the commit, and removing the first half changes nothing they can see. Only "log out, then log back in as the same user while the request is pending" needs the generation; that test does not exist (exercise 6 adds it).

Why the others are wrong:
- *Line 80 makes 99 redundant*: line 80 runs before the request; line 99 runs after it returns, when the session may have changed.
- *Vitest skips assertions in async callbacks*: the tests await their promises; the other mutations show assertions do run.
- *The tests mock the coordinator*: they use the real coordinator with mocked dependencies.

excerpts.quote: if (requestedGeneration !== this.generation || this.tokens?.user.id !== tokens.user.id) return;
The existing tests only switch to a *different* user or to logged-out (`tokens` null), so the identity half alone is enough to pass them.

notes.title: Why onCommit re-reads the outbox after committing
notes.body:
**Key: because events recorded during the request stay queued and must remain visible.**

While the request was in flight, the learner may have added event B. After the commit, the outbox in storage holds B (A was acknowledged and deleted). The array read before the request held only A. Passing that old array to `onCommit` would show A again, as if it were still pending, and would hide B. Reading the outbox again after the commit (`this.dependencies.readOutbox()` on line 103) makes the screen match what is really queued.

Why the others are wrong:
- *push mutated the array*: nothing in the code changes the batch array.
- *readOutbox is cheaper than copying*: the reason is correctness, not cost.
- *React needs a new reference*: a copy of the old array would be a new reference but still the wrong content.

excerpts.quote: this.dependencies.commit(result.progress, acknowledgedIds); this.dependencies.onCommit(result.progress, this.dependencies.readOutbox());
Publishing the pre-request array would show `A` again or hide `B`, out of step with storage.

notes.title: Server-rejected events are silently deleted
notes.body:
**Key: they are acknowledged like the rest, so they leave the outbox unreported.**

The production `push` adapter in `progress.tsx` calls `api.sync` and then builds `acknowledgedIds` from *every event it sent*: `events.map((event) => event.id)`. The `rejected` list in the server's response is never read. So rejected events are acknowledged, deleted from the outbox in the next commit, and never shown or logged. The review lists this as finding F1: deleting bad rows may be a fine policy, but it should be a visible decision.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Shown in an error banner*: no code reads `rejected`.
- *Retried forever*: they are acknowledged, so they are deleted, not kept.
- *Moved to a dead-letter table*: there is no such table.

excerpts.quote: const response = await api.sync(tokens.accessToken, events); return { progress: response.progress,
acknowledgedIds: events.map((event) => event.id),
Rejected events are deleted from the outbox and never surfaced or logged.

notes.title: Same account, new session: only the generation tells them apart
notes.body:
**Key: because the id matches again, and the generation bumped by setSession differs.**

Logging out calls `setSession(null)`, and logging back in calls `setSession(tokens)`. Each call adds 1 to `generation`. When the old response finally arrives, the user id check passes, because it is the same person. But the generation the sync started with is now two lower than the current one, so line 99 returns without committing. The request belonged to a session that ended, even if a new session for the same account exists.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The server rejects old requests*: the code does not rely on that; the guard is on the phone.
- *The id changes on each login*: user ids are stable; that is why matching them is not enough.
- *Tokens are compared*: line 99 compares the generation and the user id, not tokens.

excerpts.quote: A user can log out and later sign into the same account while an old request is still pending. The identifier matches again, but the old request belongs to a different session.
this.generation += 1;

notes.title: commitSyncedProgress replaced two separate writes
notes.body:
**Key: commitSyncedProgress, upserting baseline and deleting acked ids in one transaction.**

Originally the provider saved the baseline, then called `outboxClear` as a second step. A crash in between could leave a new baseline with old events still queued (counted twice), or the reverse. The worked change replaced both with `commitSyncedProgress`: inside `db.withTransactionSync` it upserts the baseline row and deletes only the acknowledged ids. SQLite applies the whole transaction or none of it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *An in-memory cache flushed on backgrounding*: no such cache exists.
- *The same two writes, reordered*: still two separate writes, so still not atomic.
- *A server endpoint clears the outbox*: the outbox lives on the phone; only the phone can delete from it.

excerpts.quote: for (const id of acknowledgedIds) db.runSync("DELETE FROM outbox WHERE id = ?", id);
the separate baseline write plus `outboxClear` were replaced by the single-transaction `commitSyncedProgress`

notes.title: Only acknowledgements for sent events are applied
notes.body:
**Key: only a: acks are intersected with the sent batch, so c stays queued.**

Line 100 builds a set of the ids in the batch that was sent. Line 101 keeps only the returned ids that are in that set. "a" was sent, so it stays; "c" was not (it was recorded during the request), so it is filtered out. The commit deletes only "a", and "c" will go in the next sync.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Both a and c*: the filter removes "c" before the commit.
- *The whole outbox*: the commit only deletes the ids it is given.
- *Neither, the commit aborts*: unknown ids are simply dropped from the list; nothing aborts.

excerpts.quote: const requestedIds = new Set(batch.map((event) => event.id)); const acknowledgedIds = result.acknowledgedIds.filter((id) => requestedIds.has(id));
Only identifiers present in the sent batch may be removed

notes.title: A network error with no status is simply rethrown
notes.body:
**Key: it is rethrown, with no refresh and nothing committed or acknowledged.**

In the `catch` after `push`, line 88 rethrows unless the error is an object with `status` equal to 401. A network error with no status fails that test, so `throw error` runs. The refresh, the second push, the commit and `onCommit` all come later and never run. The outbox keeps every event for the next sync, and the caller sees the failure.

Why the others are wrong:
- *A refresh is attempted*: only a 401 leads to a refresh.
- *The coordinator retries with backoff*: there is no retry loop in `runOnce`.
- *The batch is acknowledged anyway*: acknowledging without a successful push would lose events.

excerpts.quote: } catch (error) { if (!error || typeof error !== "object" || !("status" in error) || error.status !== 401) { throw error; }
Other failures propagate without pretending progress was committed.

notes.title: Why the internal queue swallows errors but the caller does not
notes.body:
**Key: after one failure, each later sync() chains onto a rejection and never runs.**

`sync()` chains each attempt after the previous one with `this.tail.then(...)`. A `.then` callback only runs if the earlier promise *succeeded*. If `this.tail` were the raw `operation` and it failed, every later `this.tail.then(() => this.runOnce(...))` would skip its callback and just pass the rejection on. Syncing would stop until the app restarts. Storing `operation.catch(() => undefined)` as the tail turns a failure into "done" for the queue, while `sync()` still returns the original `operation`, so the caller sees the error.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Syncs would run in parallel*: chaining still keeps them in order; they would never run at all.
- *The caller stops receiving rejections*: the caller gets `operation`, which still rejects.
- *Nothing important*: one failure would disable syncing.

excerpts.quote: const operation = this.tail.then(() => this.runOnce(requestedGeneration)); this.tail = operation.catch(() => undefined); return operation;
With `this.tail = operation`, the second `sync()` chains onto a rejected promise, `runOnce` never runs, and the new test **fails** (`push` called once).

notes.title: A 401 after logout does not refresh the old account
notes.body:
**Key: it returns at the generation check, without refreshing the abandoned account.**

The push failed with 401, so line 88 does not rethrow. Before calling `refresh`, line 91 checks the generation. The logout called `setSession(null)`, so the generation has moved on and `runOnce` returns quietly. No refresh request goes out for an account the user has left, and no new tokens can bring that session back. Line 93 repeats the check after a refresh, for the case where the logout happens during it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Refreshes, retries, then discards*: the check comes before the refresh, so none of that happens.
- *Clears the outbox*: nothing in this path touches storage.
- *Rethrows the 401*: a 401 takes the refresh branch, which returns instead of throwing.

excerpts.quote: if (requestedGeneration !== this.generation) return; const fresh = await this.dependencies.refresh(tokens.refreshToken); if (requestedGeneration !== this.generation) return;
These checks prevent a late unauthorized response from initiating a refresh for an abandoned account and prevent returned credentials from restoring a logged-out session.

notes.title: The ack filter is belt-and-braces in production
notes.body:
**Key: because the production adapter builds acknowledgedIds from the sent events.**

The filter on lines 100-101 removes acknowledgements for events that were not sent. But the real `push` adapter in `progress.tsx` creates `acknowledgedIds` by mapping over the very events it was given. Every id it returns is therefore in the batch, and the filter never removes anything. The review (F2) says to keep it anyway, because a future adapter might trust a server-supplied list, and to pin it with a test.

Why the others are wrong:
- *runOnce skips the filter on a first-try success*: the filter runs after every successful push.
- *The outbox is cleared before each push*: it is not; events wait until they are acknowledged.
- *TypeScript prevents other ids*: a `string[]` type cannot know which strings were in the batch.

excerpts.quote: acknowledgedIds: events.map((event) => event.id),
Because of F1's adapter, `sync.ts:100-101` can never filter anything today. Keep it (it protects against a future adapter), but pair it with the exercise-4 test so it cannot silently regress.

notes.title: One sync attempt sends at most 500 events
notes.body:
**Key: the first 500 events, via readOutbox().slice(0, 500).**

`runOnce` reads the outbox and takes `.slice(0, 500)`: elements 0 to 499. With 1,200 events queued, it sends 500, commits those that are acknowledged, and returns. The remaining 700 stay in the outbox until later `sync()` calls. There is no loop inside `runOnce`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Pages of 500 in one runOnce*: `runOnce` makes one push (two only on a 401 retry, of the same batch).
- *All 1,200 in one request*: the slice caps the batch.
- *Events since the last good sync*: the batch is simply the first 500 in the outbox, whatever their age.

excerpts.quote: const batch = this.dependencies.readOutbox().slice(0, 500);
When the operation starts, it reads at most five hundred outbox events and sends that batch with the active credentials.

notes.title: A late profile update keeps the newer tokens
notes.body:
**Key: it merges the returned user into the current tokens, not the captured ones.**

`updateMe` started with a snapshot of the session, including the access token at that time. During the request, a refresh replaced `this.tokens` with new credentials. When the profile comes back, `applyUserUpdate` first checks the generation and the user id, then sets `this.tokens = { ...this.tokens, user }`: it copies the *current* tokens and only swaps in the new user profile. The refreshed access token survives.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Replaces with the captured set*: that would restore the outdated token, which is the bug being avoided.
- *Refreshes again*: no second refresh is made.
- *Drops the update after any refresh*: the update is applied as long as the session is the same.

excerpts.quote: // Preserve credentials that may have refreshed while updateMe was in flight. this.tokens = { ...this.tokens, user };
A returned user profile may be current while its captured access token is outdated because refresh occurred in the meantime.
